svg.aria-label: Diagram: Policy Simulator against existing resources versus dry-run mode against live operations, the spec and dryRunSpec fields coexisting in one policy, the audit log query that finds would-be violations, and the constraint kinds neither tool can rehearse
svg.title: Rehearsing an organization policy: Policy Simulator, dry-run mode, and the constraints neither can test
svg.text: There is no staging environment for an organization node
Two tools compensate, and they answer different questions. Picking the wrong one gives a clean result about the wrong thing.
Policy Simulator — before anything is set
What already violates this policy?
Previews the impact of a new custom or managed
constraint before it is enforced in production.
Looks at existing resources, as they stand.
Returns the list of resources that violate it — the
remediation backlog enforcement will not fix for you,
because policies are not retroactive.
Cannot test changes to legacy managed constraints.
Dry-run mode — while it is set
What would this refuse from now on?
Created and enforced like any other policy, and
violations are audit logged — but nothing is denied.
Looks at operations, as they happen.
So it only ever sees the traffic that occurs in the
window. A quarterly job simply does not appear.
Custom, managed, and four legacy constraints only.
One policy can hold both specs
dryRunSpec:
rules:
- enforce: true
Keep spec enforcing today’s rule while dryRunSpec
measures the stricter one on real traffic.
The query that turns logs into an answer
protoPayload.metadata.dryRunResult = “DENIED”
AND protoPayload.metadata.liveResult = “ALLOWED”
The proposed rule would have refused this, and
today’s rules let it through. Every row is a workflow
that breaks on the day you promote it.
The gap is exactly where you least want it
Dry run supports custom constraints, managed constraints, and four legacy ones: restrict service usage, restrict
endpoint usage, restrict TLS versions, restrict TLS cipher suites. Any other constraint returns an error.
So the constraints easiest to adopt are the hardest to rehearse. Prefer a managed constraint partly because
it can be tested at all — and where you cannot test, spend the caution on scope instead.
The order that works
1. Simulate — get the existing violations. Fix or exempt them; this is usually the long pole.
2. Set the dry run at the scope the real policy will occupy, since it inherits to descendants like any policy.
3. Query the verdict mismatch on a schedule, and route results to the teams that own the workloads.
4. Promote by moving the rule from dryRunSpec to spec once the mismatches stop or are accepted.
Two commands that look alike and are not:
set-policy --update-mask=dryRunSpec ends the experiment and leaves the live policy enforcing.
org-policies delete removes both. During an incident that is the difference between a rollback and an outage.
